commons:98280862.summary: Christ, haloed and robed in red and blue, raises his hand toward the tomb, where Lazarus stands upright in his grave clothes, while a figure in red lies prostrate at Christ's feet. Crowds of onlookers fill the scene below a tall mountain and a turreted building. With its saturated colours and expressive figures, the Armenian miniature makes Christ's command, 'Lazarus, come forth', vivid and immediate.
facts: The Mughni Gospels (Matenadaran MS 7736) is an 11th-century Armenian Gospel book; Wikipedia dates it to 1060 and notes its 301 folios.
The miniature's Armenian caption reads 'The Resurrection of Lazarus' (per the Commons record).
commons:98280862.notes: The Commons title 'Mulna' refers to the Mughni (Mugni) Gospels, MS 7736, fol. 16v. The Commons Arabic description says 'end of the 11th century', while Wikipedia gives 1060.

cur:catacombs2-lamta-sayada-tree-sarcoph.summary: Trees with spreading crowns divide the front of this marble sarcophagus into a sequence of biblical episodes, carved with lively detail down to the dogs at the figures' feet. Near the centre a bearded Christ, raised above the others, hands an unrolled scroll to an apostle who bows to receive it, while another apostle stands on the other side, the composition that the Lamta museum describes as Christ between Peter and Paul. The lid carries hunting scenes on either side of a blank inscription panel.
facts: It was discovered west of Sayada, in the El Karaïa quarter, and is displayed with its carved marble lid in the archaeological museum of Lamta (ancient Leptiminus).
French Wikipedia describes the lid and chest as showing Christ surrounded by the apostles Paul and Peter.
cur:catacombs2-lamta-sayada-tree-sarcoph.notes: French Wikipedia calls it 'Byzantine', but the tree-sarcophagus type is characteristic of the later 4th century; the date and most side scenes were not verified.

europeana:2048087/ProvidedCHO_British_Mu.summary: This small cast crucifix, known here from the recording drawing, shows Christ in relief on the face of the cross, wearing a crown and a short skirt knotted at the waist, his arms apparently bound to the cross-arms. A broken suspension loop at the top shows that it was worn as a pendant. Found in Norfolk, it is a humble witness to personal devotion in late Anglo-Saxon England.
facts: The Portable Antiquities Scheme record compares its style with a silver crucifix from Gotland published by James Graham-Campbell in Viking Artefacts (1980) and with another find from the Isle of Wight.
The record describes the metal as worn and corroded to a purplish colour and dates the piece to the 11th century.
europeana:2048087/ProvidedCHO_British_Mu.notes: Description and date taken from the PAS record as served by Europeana; the PAS site itself blocked direct access. The worklist date '1000' was the aggregator's sort value; the record text says 11th century. The image is a line drawing, not a photograph.

walters:41.228.summary: Carved in soft green-grey steatite, this small fragment shows the Virgin with a large, wide-eyed face framed by her veil, holding the Christ Child before her. The Child, with a halo and a youthful, serious face, sits on her lap with his robe carved in scale-like folds. Although broken at the edges, it keeps the frontal, solemn presence of Byzantine icons of the Mother of God.
facts: The Walters dates the carving to the 9th century and attributes it to Byzantium; it is only 7.4 cm high.
It was owned by Henry Walters and later by the dealer Joseph Brummer, and was given to the museum in 1941 by Miss Julia R. Rogers of Baltimore.
walters:41.228.notes: The 9th-century date is the museum's; Byzantine steatite icons are more often dated to the 10th–12th centuries, so the date may deserve review.

feat:gabelkreuz-st-maria-im-kapitol.summary: Hung on a Y-shaped cross shaped like a living tree, this emaciated Christ — ribs protruding, limbs contorted, body covered in wounds — is one of the most harrowing images of the Passion ever made. It belongs to the 'Crucifixus dolorosus' type that spread through the Rhineland soon after 1300, inviting the faithful into intense compassion with the suffering Savior. Such images grew out of the Passion-centred mystical piety of the age; despite the later nickname 'plague cross', the type appeared decades before the Black Death.
facts: The forked shape of the cross recalls a living tree, linking the Crucifixion with the trees of Paradise — read as the Tree of Life or the Tree of Knowledge whose sin Christ's suffering overcomes.
Tradition long dated the cross to 1304; it was certainly made before 1312. Recent restoration uncovered mostly a late-medieval second paint layer, with small areas of the original colouring.
Long thought to be the oldest forked crucifix of all, it is now seen rather as the work that popularized the type in the Rhineland; another early example hangs in St. Severin in Cologne.
Its style has little in common with Cologne sculpture of its day, and Italian influence is evident, leading scholars to suggest an itinerant or foreign-trained carver working in local walnut.
